'And Jacob abode there that night, and he sent away from him all his flocks and all his possessions to his father Isaac and to his mother Rebecca. And Jacob tithed all the clean animals, and made a burnt-offering, and he gave the tithe to Levi his son, and the second tithe he ate himself before the Lord' — Jubilees uniquely preserves Jacob's institution of the tithe-of-tithes pattern (one tithe to the priest, one tithe consumed by the offerer before the Lord) as a pre-Mosaic patriarchal ordinance. The Tewahedo monastic ǝʾǝsär practice (one tithe to the church / priesthood, a second consumed in festive remembrance) draws canonical anchor here: the Levitical tithe and the ma'aser-šeni (festive tithe consumed by the offerer) are BOTH patriarchal, not just Deut-15-Mosaic. The Tewahedo's distinctive double-tithe practice is canonically pre-Mosaic in this framing.

The Tewahedo monastic practice of planting trees at the gravesites of beloved spiritual mothers (including nurses, deaconesses, female monastics) has its canonical anchor in Deborah's Bethel oak: the burial-tree as living memorial.

'And he was a great burden to her in her travail, and his soul came near to depart from her, and she had hardly delivered him when she died. And she called his name "son of my sorrow," but Jacob his father called his name Benjamin' — Rachel dies in childbirth bearing Benjamin (Gen 35:18 parallel). Jubilees preserves the doubled naming (Ben-oni / Benjamin). Tewahedo readings see in the doubled naming the canonical type of suffering-transmuted-into-joy: the mother's last word names the cost of motherhood; the father's name names the elevation of the cost into covenantal gladness. The Tewahedo Marian theology of suffering-with-Christ-as-redemptive-fellowship (cf. Lk 2:35 sword-piercing Mary's soul) draws on this canonical matriarchal pattern: the cost of bearing is real AND is renamed by covenantal interpretation.
